steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
1. The increase in rush-hour traffic flow "would not have occurred had the city not invested in computer modeling technology."
no investment → no increase in rush-hour flow
increase in rush-hour flow → investment (contrapositive)

2. The financial predicament "would not have been resolved if the traffic flow across the bridge during rush hour had not been increased."
no increase in rush-hour flow → predicament not resolved
predicament resolved → increase in rush-hour flow (contrapositive)

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Both sentences are conditionals, and they share one idea: the increase in rush-hour traffic flow. When two rules share a term, try to chain them.

The increase is the result in the first rule and the trigger in the second:
no investment → no increase in rush-hour flow → predicament not resolved

Read it forward: without the computer modeling investment, there's no increase, and without the increase, the predicament stays unresolved. Or read the contrapositive: resolving the predicament required the increase, and the increase required the investment.

Each link is a requirement. The investment was needed; nothing says it was enough. So the safe inferences are about what could not have happened without something, not about what was guaranteed to happen.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for the two ends of the chain joined together. Something like: if the city had not invested in computer modeling technology, the financial predicament would not have been resolved. The contrapositive version (resolving the predicament required the investment) would work just as well.

notes.body: The rules only require that the city invest in computer modeling technology. Buying a competing package is still investing in computer modeling technology, so the requirement would be met. And meeting a requirement doesn't guarantee anything, so we can't say the predicament would have stayed unresolved.

This is the chain with the middle link removed. No investment means no rush-hour increase (sentence one), and no increase means the predicament isn't resolved (sentence two). So no investment means no resolution.

The move to repeat: when two conditionals share a term, line them up so the shared term is the result of one and the trigger of the other, then connect the outer ends. Check the direction too. B keeps the "not" on both sides in the same order the rules give them, so it follows.

The stimulus only tells us about rush-hour flow. Daily totals could still fall if off-peak traffic dropped. It also never compares this year with last year. Rush-hour flow went up, but we aren't told when, so the year-over-year comparison has no support.

The requirement was the investment, made "at the request of the city's mayor." Nothing says the mayor made it "the highest budgetary priority." The city could have invested as a modest line item and the increase would still have happened, so the mayor's top-priority ranking was never needed.

We know the mayor requested the investment, but we're never told why. The mayor might have wanted it for something else entirely, and the traffic gain could have been a side effect. A motive is a new claim, and nothing in the rules supports it.

why: The only step was a garbled one-word-per-line diagram with no chaining or prediction, the correct note was a bare diagram, and A, D and E were verdict-only.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
Coastal estuaries are easily polluted by nutrient-rich sewage.

When that pollution overnutrifies the water, algae proliferate.
sewage overnutrifies water → algae proliferate

The abundant algae "sometimes" feed microorganisms that are toxic to fish, killing most of the fish.
abundant algae → (sometimes) toxic microorganisms thrive → most fish die

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Each sentence picks up where the last one ended: sewage leads to overnutrified water, overnutrified water leads to algae, and algae can lead to a fish kill. When causes and effects line up end to end like this, connect the first cause to the last effect.

Watch the word "sometimes" on the last link. The algae don't always feed toxic microorganisms. So the chain doesn't prove that sewage always kills the fish. It proves that it can.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for a softly worded answer that joins the start of the chain to the end: overnutrifying an estuary with sewage can lead to most of its fish dying. An answer that says this "will" happen goes past the "sometimes".

notes.body: This compares sewage pollution with pollution "in some other way." The stimulus never mentions any other kind of pollution, so we have nothing to compare against. Even for sewage, the fish kill only happens "sometimes," so we can't rank sewage as the deadlier pollutant.

The stimulus says the algae give toxic microorganisms "a rich food source." It says nothing about how fast those microorganisms reproduce or how they compare with other microorganisms. Plenty of food for one group doesn't prove that group outgrows all the others.

The stimulus describes one way sewage can harm fish: the algae it produces feed microorganisms that are toxic to fish. It never rules out other kinds of harm, so saying sewage does not harm fish "in any way other than" this one goes too far.

Sewage pollution is one way to get algae to proliferate. Nothing says it's the only way. D treats a cause as a requirement. Test it: an estuary with no sewage that gets nutrients from farm runoff could still fill with algae, and nothing in the stimulus says otherwise.

This connects the first cause to the final effect: sewage overnutrifies the water, the water grows algae, and the algae sometimes feed microorganisms that kill most of the fish.

The word "can" is what makes it safe. Because the last link only happens "sometimes," the chain proves possibility, not certainty. When a chain has a weak link, the right answer keeps that weakness in its wording.

why: No Evaluate or Goal, the diagram dropped the "sometimes" that makes E's "can" correct, and A, B, D and the correct note were verdict-only or bare.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
Some nurseries label any Stark Sweet Melody nectarine trees "miniature." Others do not.

Rule: if a variety of fruit tree is not suitable for growing in a tub or a pot, no tree of that variety can be correctly labeled miniature.
variety not suitable for tub or pot → no tree of it is correctly labeled "miniature"
correctly labeled "miniature" → variety suitable for tub or pot (contrapositive)

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
We have one rule and one fact. The rule works on a variety's suitability. The fact is about one variety: some nurseries call every Stark Sweet Melody tree "miniature."

Can we fire the rule? Only if we know whether Stark Sweet Melody is suitable for a tub or pot, and we're never told. So we can't say anyone is mislabeling outright.

What we can do is put the inference in conditional form. Suppose Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable. Then none of its trees can be correctly labeled "miniature." But some nurseries label them "miniature." So those nurseries are mislabeling.

Also notice what the rule doesn't give us. Suitability is required for a correct "miniature" label, but it isn't enough. Even a suitable variety might not be miniature.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that keeps the unknown as a condition: "If Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable for a tub or pot, then some nurseries are mislabeling it." It might be phrased with "unless," which means "if not."

notes.body: "Most nurseries" is a claim about the whole industry. The stimulus only tells us about some nurseries and one variety, and we don't even know whether that variety is mislabeled. Nothing supports a count of most.

B says a correct label requires the variety to be unsuitable. The rule points the other way: a correct "miniature" label requires that the variety be suitable. And if the variety is suitable, nothing stops the "miniature" labels from being correct, so correct labeling clearly doesn't depend on unsuitability.

This is the tempting one. It's true only if Stark Sweet Melody is unsuitable for a tub or pot, and the stimulus never says so. If the variety is suitable, the rule doesn't fire and the "miniature" labels might be correct. C states as fact what E correctly keeps as a condition.

The rule only says when a "miniature" label can't be correct. It never says when a tree must be labeled "miniature." Suitability is a requirement, not a guarantee, so no tree is ever shown to deserve the label. We can't prove that leaving it off is a mistake.

"Unless X, Y" means "if not X, then Y." So E says: if Stark Sweet Melody is not suitable for a tub or pot, some nurseries mislabel it. That's our prediction. An unsuitable variety can't be correctly labeled "miniature," and some nurseries label it "miniature," so those nurseries are wrong.

The move to repeat: when the fact you need to fire a rule is missing, look for an answer that turns the missing fact into an "if" (or an "unless").

why: No real breakdown or prediction on a d3 conditional, B and the correct note carried garbled diagrams, and A, C and D were verdict-only.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
- One should not do anything that has the potential to produce serious harm to one's society.
  - The public actions, or inactions, of celebrities and of people who are widely respected are widely emulated.
  - Some celebrities do not vote.
  - Serious harm befalls a society in which many people refrain from voting.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Look for ideas that show up in more than one statement and chain them.

Public inactions of widely respected people are widely emulated. Not voting is an inaction. So if a widely respected person publicly refrains from voting, many people may refrain too. Many people refraining brings serious harm. That gives us a chain:
widely respected person publicly doesn't vote → many people don't vote → serious harm to society

Now the first statement applies. Publicly not voting has the potential to produce serious harm, so one should not do it.

Notice what the chain does not need: the third statement. "Some celebrities do not vote" doesn't say they do it publicly, so it doesn't fire anything. It's there to tempt you into an answer about celebrities who don't vote.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for a "should not" principle about people whose actions are emulated: widely respected people (or celebrities) should not publicly refrain from voting. Be wary of answers that tell society what to require, tell people whom to respect or emulate, or tell anyone they must vote. The stimulus only says what one should not do.

notes.body: The stimulus only tells individuals what they "should not do." It never says what a society should require. And the harm comes from public inaction being emulated, so a celebrity who quietly skips voting threatens nothing. Nothing supports forcing every celebrity to vote.

This makes voting itself need a justification. The stimulus never says voting causes harm, so the first principle gives no reason to hold back from voting. Worse, B would tell an ordinary person whose vote won't inspire anyone not to vote, which pushes toward the harm the stimulus warns about.

The stimulus says respected people are emulated. It never says who deserves respect. Whether non-voting celebrities should lose respect is a new judgment, and none of the statements has the power to prove it.

The stimulus describes who gets emulated; it never tells anyone whom to emulate. It also says nothing about celebrities who are not widely respected. D mixes the stimulus's words into an instruction to a different audience about a group the stimulus never discusses.

This is the chain's end. Widely respected people's public inactions are emulated, so if they publicly don't vote, many may follow. Many people not voting brings serious harm, and one should not do anything with that potential.

E also gets the scope right. It doesn't say anyone must vote, only that they shouldn't refrain publicly, which is exactly what the emulation statement makes risky. On a principle-inference question, the right answer's "should" usually comes straight from a "should" in the stimulus, applied to the case the other statements set up.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes and 80 to 100 word notes, the Given dropped "or inactions" (the key to applying emulation to not voting), and the Goal named only the task.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
1. No new course will be approved unless the committee or Dean Wilson has already received a proposal for it.
new course approved → proposal received by committee or by Dean Wilson

2. Dean Wilson has received only one new course proposal.

3. All new course proposals the committee has received are for upper-level courses.
committee proposal → upper-level

4. Beginning next year, all upper-level courses will have prerequisites.
upper-level → prerequisite

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Statements 3 and 4 chain together:
committee proposal → upper-level → prerequisite

Now combine that with statement 1. Every new course next year came from one of two places. If it came from the committee, it has a prerequisite. If it came from Dean Wilson, we know nothing about it, but statement 2 says the dean has only one proposal.

So the dean's pile can supply at most one new course. Every other new course must come from the committee, and so must have a prerequisite. Put plainly: at most one new course next year can lack a prerequisite.

Also notice what's missing. Receiving a proposal is required for approval, but nothing says any proposal will be approved. And the prerequisite rule covers upper-level courses only, not every course.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer built on the "at most one exception" idea: if there are two or more new courses, at least one has a prerequisite. Equivalently, any new course that didn't come from Dean Wilson's proposal has a prerequisite. Reject answers that assume a proposal gets approved, or that stretch the prerequisite rule past upper-level courses.

notes.body: The rule is upper-level → prerequisite. A reads it as if only upper-level courses can have prerequisites. With no new upper-level courses, the only possible new course is Dean Wilson's, and nothing says a lower-level course can't have a prerequisite. That's a negated conditional, and it doesn't follow.

Nothing in the stimulus makes any proposal get approved. A proposal is a requirement for approval, not a guarantee. Test it: the committee received five proposals, two were approved, and both new courses are upper-level. B's trigger is met and its result is false.

Two or more new courses can't all come from Dean Wilson, who has only one proposal. So at least one came from the committee. Committee proposals are all upper-level, and upper-level courses next year have prerequisites. So at least one new course has a prerequisite.

The move to repeat: when a rule offers two sources and one is capped at a single item, ask what happens once you need more than that cap. The extra items have to come from the other source, and everything you know about that source applies to them.

Even if every new course is upper-level and has a prerequisite, "all courses offered next year" includes courses that already exist. The prerequisite rule covers upper-level courses only, so existing lower-level courses could run without prerequisites.

With no new upper-level courses, the committee's proposals clearly weren't approved. That tells us nothing about Dean Wilson's proposal. Maybe it was approved, maybe nothing new was approved at all. Approval is never guaranteed by anything in the stimulus.

why: No Goal step, inline diagrams run together in the Given, a gendered pronoun for Dean Wilson in the correct note, em dashes in D and E, and wrong-answer notes padded in the PT157 register.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
"Moral excellence can be achieved only by repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do the wrong thing."
moral excellence → repeatedly overcame inclinations to do wrong

Overcoming these inclinations is often difficult, even for a morally virtuous person.

"The only way to become a morally virtuous person is through the achievement of moral excellence."
morally virtuous → moral excellence

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Two requirement rules share a term: moral excellence. It's the result of the virtue rule and the trigger of the excellence rule, so they chain:
morally virtuous → moral excellence → repeatedly overcame inclinations to do wrong

So every morally virtuous person has repeatedly overcome inclinations to do the wrong thing. Now take one more small step. You can't overcome an inclination you never had. So every morally virtuous person has had inclinations to do wrong.

The arrows only run one way. Moral excellence is required for virtue, not enough for it. Overcoming inclinations is required for excellence, not enough for it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Expect the end of the chain, said about virtuous people: every morally virtuous person has repeatedly overcome, and so has had, inclinations to do wrong. Watch for answers that run an arrow backward or negate both sides.

notes.body: Overcoming an inclination means resisting it, not losing the ability to act on it. The stimulus even says overcoming is "often difficult to do, even for a morally virtuous person," which suggests virtuous people still feel the pull. Nothing makes them "incapable" of doing wrong.

The rule says virtue requires excellence. It doesn't say excellence produces virtue. Plenty of people could achieve moral excellence and never become virtuous, so we can't say how many of them are virtuous, let alone "most."

C treats having no wrong inclinations as enough for moral excellence. The stimulus only gives a requirement for excellence: repeatedly overcoming such inclinations. A requirement never guarantees anything, and a person with nothing to overcome hasn't shown they met even that requirement.

This is the most tempting trap. The rule is virtuous → excellence. D says not virtuous → no excellence, which negates both sides without flipping them. The valid contrapositive is no excellence → not virtuous. Excellence is required for virtue, not limited to people who are already virtuous, so a non-virtuous person achieving it is consistent with every statement.

Chain the two rules: virtue requires excellence, and excellence requires repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do wrong. So every virtuous person has overcome such inclinations, and you can't overcome an inclination you never had.

The move to repeat: when two "only" rules share a term, connect the outer ends, then ask what the final requirement itself presupposes. The right answer here states that presupposition.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes; the B note claimed we can infer some excellent people are virtuous (not guaranteed), the C note overclaimed a contradiction, and the Evaluate offered a shaky "often difficult" inference as a prediction.

steps.label: Given
steps.body:
- Some recently invented television screens are built out of small tiles seamlessly joined together.
  - Each tile is a separate miniature screen.
  - Television sets with these compound screens are just a few inches thick.
  - For a noncompound screen in a set of this thickness, the larger the screen is, the dimmer it is.
  - However, each tile in a compound screen is small enough to be quite bright.
  - Moreover, an unlimited number of the tiles can be joined together, without making the resulting screen any less bright or the set any thicker.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The report sets up a problem and then a fix. The problem: in a set a few inches thick, a noncompound screen gets dimmer as it gets larger, so thin, large and bright don't go together. The fix: compound screens are made of small, bright tiles, and you can add as many tiles as you want without losing brightness or adding thickness.

Put those together. Keep adding tiles and the screen gets as large as you like, stays bright, and the set stays a few inches thick. So thin sets with screens that are both bright and very large are now possible.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for the fix stated as a capability: thin television sets can now have screens that are both large and bright. The "However" and "Moreover" tell us the report is building toward exactly that. Reject answers about what people want, what's wrong with the new screens, or how thickness changes brightness.

notes.body: Nothing in the report counts against small screens. It says unlimited tiles can be joined, not that a screen needs many tiles. A compound screen of just a few bright tiles fits everything we're told.
The report is about what the technology can do, not what buyers want. Test it: every sentence could be true even if nobody wanted to buy one of these sets. Demand is a new topic.

The report describes size and brightness at one fixed thickness: "a set of this thickness." It never changes the thickness, so it can't tell us what a thicker set does to brightness. C invents a second relationship from a sentence that held thickness constant.

This is the problem and the fix put together. Noncompound screens in thin sets get dimmer as they grow. Compound screens are thin, each tile is bright, and unlimited tiles can be added without losing brightness or adding thickness. So a thin set can now have a screen that's both bright and very large.

The move to repeat: when a stimulus states a limitation and then says "however" and "moreover" about a new approach, the inference is usually that the new approach gets past that limitation.

The report lists advantages. It never says those are the only differences. Cost, resolution or visible seams could all be worse with compound screens, and nothing in the report rules that out. Silence about disadvantages doesn't prove there are none.

why: No Goal step, wrong-answer notes were thin and lacked tests, and the correct note restated the stimulus in the PT157 register without teaching the move.

steps.label: Statements
steps.body:
Rule (if):
based on info from a reliable source → reasonable to maintain

Fact (some): some beliefs are
1. based on info from a reliable source, and
2. not self-evident, and
3. not grounded in observable evidence

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
We have one conditional and one fact. With a conditional on Must Be True, ask two questions:
1. Is there another conditional to chain it with?
2. Does any fact trigger it (or its contrapositive)?

There's no second conditional, so #1 is out. For #2, the "some" beliefs in the second sentence are based on information from a reliable source. That triggers the rule, so those beliefs are reasonable to maintain.

Now that group has four traits at once: reliable source, reasonable, not self-evident, and not grounded in observable evidence. The question is most likely testing whether we can attach "reasonable" to the other traits in that group.

Two limits to keep in mind. A "some" fact is about one group, so it can't become a rule about all beliefs. And the rule only says a reliable source is enough for reasonableness, not that it's the only route.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for a "some" statement that pairs reasonable with one or both of the other traits: some reasonable beliefs are not self-evident, some reasonable beliefs are not grounded in observable evidence, or some reasonable beliefs are neither.

notes.body: The stimulus proves the opposite for some beliefs. The beliefs in the second sentence aren't grounded in observable evidence, yet they come from a reliable source and so are reasonable. A belief can lack observable evidence and still be reasonable.

The second sentence directly contradicts this. It describes beliefs that are based on a reliable source and are not self-evident. One counterexample is enough to sink an "all" claim, and the stimulus hands us that counterexample.

The rule runs reliable source → reasonable. C runs it backward: reasonable (with no observable evidence) → reliable source. A reliable source is one way to make a belief reasonable, not the only way. A reasonable belief could rest on something else entirely.

This turns a "some" fact into a rule. The second sentence shows some beliefs lack both traits, but a group that lacks both doesn't prove that lacking one forces lacking the other. Nothing rules out a belief that is self-evident yet not grounded in observable evidence.

Run the beliefs from the second sentence through the rule. They're based on a reliable source, so they're reasonable. They're also not self-evident and not grounded in observable evidence. So among reasonable beliefs that aren't self-evident, some aren't grounded in observable evidence.

The move to repeat: when a "some" fact triggers a rule, the rule's result attaches to that group, and you can pair it with any other trait the group has. The right answer is often a "some" statement built from those traits.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes and 100-word notes; the diagram lost its layout; A said the stimulus is silent when it actually disproves A; the Goal missed that E pairs reasonable with both traits.
